ci-two-proportions-s1.title: App use at city and rural stores
ci-two-proportions-s1.text: A grocery chain takes a random sample of 300 shoppers at its city stores and a separate random sample of 220 shoppers at its rural stores. It asks each shopper whether they order with the chain's app. (Invented data.)

ci-two-proportions-s2.title: Text or call reminders
ci-two-proportions-s2.text: A dental office has 240 patients with appointments next month. It randomly assigns 120 to get a text reminder and 120 to get a phone call. It records who keeps the appointment. (Invented data.)

items.q: What is the point estimate of $p_C - p_R$, the difference between the true proportions of city and rural shoppers who use the app?

options: That is the proportion for both samples together, $\frac{279}{520}$. It mixes the groups instead of comparing them.
That averages the two sample proportions. The estimate of a difference is a difference.
That subtracts the counts, $180 - 99$. The samples have different sizes, so compare proportions, not counts.

items.q: Which statement correctly checks the large counts condition for a confidence interval for $p_C - p_R$?

why.correct: An interval uses $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$: $n_1\hat{p}_1$, $n_1(1 - \hat{p}_1)$, $n_2\hat{p}_2$, $n_2(1 - \hat{p}_2)$ are each at least 10.
options: Right: for an interval, use the observed successes and failures in each sample: $300 - 180 = 120$ and $220 - 99 = 121$.
There is no reason to use 0.5. An interval uses each sample's own $\hat{p}$.
That is not the condition. The counts of successes and failures must each reach 10.
Comparing $n$ with 30 is not the check for proportions. Count successes and failures in each sample.
The counts 180, 120, 99 and 121 are each at least 10
Each sample proportion is between 0.1 and 0.9
The two sample sizes, 300 and 220, are each at least 30

items.q: What is the standard error of $\hat{p}_C - \hat{p}_R$? Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: You added the two standard errors. Add the two variance terms under one square root.
That is the sum of the variances. Take its square root to get the standard error.

items.q: Construct a 95% confidence interval for $p_C - p_R$. Give each end to three decimal places.
Interpret the 95% interval from 0.064 to 0.236 in context.

why.correct: Name the level, the interval and the parameter in context: the true difference, city minus rural.

options: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.064 to 0.236 captures
There is a 95% chance that the sample difference is between 0.064 and 0.236, which is
95% of shoppers fall between 0.064 and 0.236, which describes

why.1: The sample difference is 0.15 for certain. Confidence is about the true difference, which the interval may or may not capture.
why.2: An interval for a proportion says nothing about individual shoppers; it estimates a parameter.

options: the true difference in the proportions of city and rural shoppers who use the app (city minus rural)
the difference in the two sample proportions, 0.60 minus 0.45
the true proportion of the chain's shoppers who use the app

why.1: We know the sample difference exactly; an interval estimates the population difference.
why.2: The interval is for a difference between two groups, not one overall proportion.

conclude.model: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.064 to 0.236 captures the true difference in the proportions of all city shoppers and all rural shoppers who use the app (city minus rural).

items.q: The office wants a confidence interval for $p_T - p_C$. Which condition takes the place of "two independent random samples" here?

why.correct: Random assignment creates two groups that differ only by chance, so the two-sample z interval applies.
options: Right: in an experiment, random assignment to two groups plays the role of two independent random samples.
Careful counting matters, but the condition for inference is the random assignment.
The patients were not sampled from a larger population, so the 10% condition is not the point. Random assignment is.
Equal group sizes are convenient but not needed. What matters is how patients got into the groups.
The patients were randomly assigned to the two reminder types
The office counted the kept appointments with care
The 240 patients are less than 10% of the dental patients in the region
Each group has the same number of patients, 120

items.q: What critical value $z^*$ is used for a 90% confidence interval? Give three decimal places.

why.correct: Leave 5% in each tail: $z^* = 1.645$, the 95th percentile of the standard normal distribution.

mistakes.why: That leaves 10% in one tail. For 90% confidence, 5% is in each tail, so use the 95th percentile.
That is $z^*$ for 95% confidence. For 90%, use 1.645.

items.q: Write the expression for a 90% confidence interval for $p_T - p_C$, with the values substituted.

mistakes.why: That uses $z^* = 1.96$, the 95% value. A 90% interval uses 1.645.
That adds two standard errors. The two variance terms go under one square root.
That pools the two groups. An interval does not assume the proportions are equal, so it keeps each group's own $\hat{p}$.

items.q: In this experiment, what does "90% confident" mean?

why.correct: The confidence level is the long-run capture rate of the method.
options: That is a sample result (104 of 120 is about 87%), not the meaning of the confidence level.
The sample difference is always the center of its own interval. Confidence is about capturing the true difference.
Right: the level describes the method's long-run success rate.
The true difference is fixed; this interval either captures it or not. The 90% describes the method.
About 90% of the patients who got a text kept their appointment
The difference in the sample proportions will be inside the interval 90% of the time
About 90% of intervals made this way, over many repetitions, capture the true difference
There is a 90% chance that the true difference is between the two ends of this one interval

items.q: What does the design of this study allow the office to conclude from the interval?

why.correct: Random assignment supports cause; random sampling supports generalizing. This study has the first.
options: Random sampling is for generalizing. Random assignment is what supports cause and effect, and this study has it.
Right: random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion. The patients were not a random sample, so generalize with care.
The comparison is between the two groups; both groups are needed to say the reminder type made the difference.
The 240 patients were not randomly sampled from all dental patients, so the conclusion is limited to patients like these.
Nothing about cause, because no random sample was taken
A difference between the groups can be blamed on the reminder type, for patients like these
A cause-and-effect conclusion, but just for the 120 text patients
The results apply to dental patients across the country

items.q: A researcher takes independent random samples of 400 nurses and 350 teachers and asks whether each works a second job. She wants to estimate how much the true proportions differ. Which procedure fits?

why.correct: Estimate a difference of two proportions with a two-sample z interval.
options: Overlap of two intervals is a rough and misleading comparison. One interval for the difference answers the question directly.
Right: two independent random samples, a categorical variable, and an estimate of a difference.
Nothing here is about 0.5, and the goal is to estimate, not to test one proportion.
Combining the samples estimates one overall proportion. The question compares two groups.
Two one-sample z intervals, checked for overlap
A two-sample z interval for $p_N - p_T$
A one-proportion z test of $H_0: p = 0.5$
A one-sample z interval for $p$, using the 750 people combined

items.q: A 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ goes from 0.02 to 0.14. Using the same data, how would a 99% interval compare?

why.correct: Margin of error $= z^* \times \text{SE}$; a 99% $z^*$ is larger.
options: Right: a higher level uses a larger $z^*$ (2.576 instead of 1.96), so the margin of error grows; the center is still $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$.
More confidence needs a wider net: $z^*$ rises from 1.96 to 2.576.
The data fix the standard error, but the critical value changes with the level.
The center is the sample difference, which does not change with the level.
It would be wider, with the same center of 0.08
It would be narrower, with the same center of 0.08
It would be the same width, since the data are the same
It would be wider, with a new center

items.q: A polling group plans a two-sample z interval for $p_1 - p_2$. If it takes four times as many people in both samples, about what happens to the margin of error, assuming the sample proportions stay about the same?

why.correct: The margin of error shrinks like $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$.
options: More data gives a more precise estimate, not a less precise one.
The variance is cut to a quarter, but the margin of error depends on its square root.
Larger samples give less variable statistics, so the margin shrinks.
Right: each variance term is divided by 4, so the standard error is divided by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
It doubles
It is cut to about a quarter
It stays about the same
It is cut about in half

items.q: Independent random samples give $\hat{p}_1 = 0.42$ with $n_1 = 500$ and $\hat{p}_2 = 0.35$ with $n_2 = 450$. What is the margin of error of a 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$? Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the standard error alone. The margin of error is $z^* \times \text{SE}$, with $z^* = 1.96$.
That uses $z^* = 1.645$, the 90% value. For 95%, use 1.96.

items.q: A 95% confidence interval for $p_A - p_B$ is from $-0.12$ to $-0.03$. What is the 95% interval for $p_B - p_A$ from the same data?

why.correct: Multiply both ends by $-1$ and put the smaller one first.
options: Right: switching the order changes every sign, so the ends swap and flip: $-(-0.03) = 0.03$ and $-(-0.12) = 0.12$.
Write the lower end first: from 0.03 to 0.12.
Subtracting in the other order changes the sign of the difference, so the interval moves to the other side of 0.
Those are the same two numbers in reverse order. The signs change too.
From 0.03 to 0.12
From 0.12 to 0.03

items.q: A student interprets a 95% interval for $p_C - p_R$ from 0.064 to 0.236 this way: "95% of city shoppers use the app between 6.4 and 23.6 percentage points more than rural shoppers." What is the main error?

why.correct: An interval for $p_1 - p_2$ is about the true difference in the two population proportions.
options: Writing 95% is fine. The error is what the student says the 95% refers to.
The order city minus rural is fine as long as it is stated. The error is about individuals.
An interval is centered at the sample difference, 0.15. Nothing about 0 is needed to interpret it.
Right: the interval is about the true difference in proportions; "95% of shoppers" describes individuals, which an interval for a proportion never does.
A confidence level is not allowed to be written as a percent
The ends should be in the order rural minus city
The interval should have been centered at 0
The interval estimates one population difference, not how individual shoppers behave

items.q: A school compares two programs. In a random sample of 25 students from program A, 22 passed a test; in a random sample of 30 from program B, 26 passed. Why is a two-sample z interval not appropriate?

why.correct: Successes and failures in each sample must each be at least 10.
options: Close proportions are fine to compare. The problem is the counts.
Different sample sizes are fine. The problem is the small numbers of failures.
Right: the large counts condition fails, so the sampling distribution may not be approximately normal.
Random samples are what we want. The problem is too few failures in each sample.
The pass rates, 0.88 and 0.87, are too close together to compare
The two samples have different sizes, 25 and 30
Sample A has 3 failures and sample B has 4, fewer than 10
The samples are random, so the results are not reliable
